results.content: 25 Types of assumptions • Presumed mechanisms of missing data – MCAR, MAR, MNAR • Analytic models involve – Analysis populations (efficacy, safety, etc.) – Distributional assumptions (mean, variance, parametric family) – Form of modeled variables (linear, dichotomized, interactions) – Auxiliary variables included in missing data models – Departures from MAR or MNAR assumptions 26 Guiding Principles • Maintain RCT / regulatory standards – Per randomization analyses – Pre-specification of analysis methods – Try for analysis obtained if no missing data occurred • Estimands, estimates, inferential methods • Avoid unnecessary assumptions – Avoid (semi)parametric assumptions across treatment arms • Minimize dimensionality of untestable assumptions – “Don’t make up 14 numbers to arrive at 1 made up number” • “Tipping point” analyses to identify limits of evidence 27 Primary Analysis • Addresses missing data: typically MAR, but perhaps MNAR – E.g., presume 30 day survival following hospital discharge • Relatively distribution-free probability model – Distribution-free interpretation of common analysis methods • Preserves weighting used in absence of missing data • Analysis method treats MAR as special case of MNAR • All of above easily addressed using multiple imputation – Also relatively transparent assumptions 28 Framework for Sensitivity Analyses • Separate MNAR parameters for each treatment arm • Assume average MNAR ”effect” across modeled baseline covariates • Tipping point analyses (using contour plots?) for p values, CI – Based on minimal parameterization of MNAR • Descriptive analyses of missing data – Exploration of stratum specific MNAR ”effects” that correspond to average MNAR ”effects” reported in tipping point analyses 29 Reporting Analyses • Devote much attention to descriptive statistics that might – Indicate the magnitude of data that had to be imputed – Support the reasoning behind particular sensitivity analyses • Descriptive statistics overall and by missingness patterns – Baseline (pre-randomization) – Treatment administered: dose delays, reductions, holidays, d/c – Patient disposition: d/c drug, d/c assessments, withdraw consent • Perhaps time to d/c or withdrawal by important predictors – Any interim measures of primary, secondary, safety outcomes • Provide primary analysis inference and summarize tipping points – Summarize how more detailed assumptions might translate to parameterizations used in sensitivity analyses 30 Example: Methotrexate in PBC • Combes, et al, Hepatology, 2005 – Issues with stopping study drug, clinic visits, or all follow-up Example: Methotrexate in PBC • Premature discontinuation of clinic visits – Missing time to subclinical progression of hyperbilirubinemia • Compare those with / without premature discontinuation – Baseline characteristics – Most recent bilirubin levels – Trends in bilirubin levels – (But interested in patterns of bilirubin after discontinuation) 31 32 Methods of Analyzing Data An Example Where am I going?

results.title: Missing Data Imputation | Brett Klamer
results.content: There are four common methods for handling missing data 1) complete case analysis, 2) single dataset imputation, 3) multiple dataset imputation, and 4) fully Bayesian imputation. - When data are missing in X and not MCAR (MAR or MNAR), it will produce biased estimates of means, regression coefficients, regression covariance. 2. If missing in X, and you have data that may explain why those values are missing (MAR), use multiple imputation (or a ‘nice’ single imputation method if simplicity is more important) where the imputation model includes both Y and the variables related to missingness. 3. If missing in Y, or X and Y, and you have data that may explain why those values are missing, use multiple imputation.

results.title: Types of missing data in data analysis: theoretical background | by Dima Diachkov | Data And Beyond | Medium
results.content: # Types of missing data in data analysis: theoretical background. Missing data must be one of the most common challenges real-world data professionals face, and handling it can make or break your analysis. However, not many analytics distinguish different missing data mechanisms, namely so-called: **MCAR**, **MAR**, and **MNAR**. Is your data missing completely at random (MCAR), where the absence is purely coincidental? Perhaps, more worryingly, it’s missing not at random (MNAR), where the missingness is intertwined with unobserved values that are critical to your analysis. In this article, we’ll peel back these layers of the missing data mechanisms and show you why identifying the cause of missingness is more than an academic exercise — it’s the key to choosing the right strategy for handling it. The examples of each of 3 types of missing data are:. The data is considered MCAR because the gaps are purely coincidental, and the missing values do not introduce bias into the analysis. Since the mechanism driving the missingness is tied to the missing values themselves, handling MNAR requires external data sources, such as tax records or specialized assumptions about the nature of the missing data. * **Handling**: ***Simple techniques like complete-case analysis (removing rows with missing data) or imputing with the mean are valid and do not introduce bias.***. * **Key Property**: Missingness depends on observed data but not the missing values themselves. * **Handling**: ***Imputation methods, such as regression-based imputation or multiple imputation, can effectively address MAR by using observed data to predict missing values.***. * **Key Property**: Missingness depends on the unobserved (missing) data. * **Impact**: Direct analysis of the observed data is biased because the missing data mechanism is tied to the missing values themselves. Assumptions and analysis planning in studies with missing data in multiple variables: moving beyond the MCAR/MAR/MNAR classification. MCAR, MAR, and MNAR values in the same dataset: a realistic evaluation of methods for handling missing data. Handling missing data in clinical research. Missing data, if not handled properly, can distort your analysis, lead to biased conclusions, and undermine decision-making. When data is missing purely by chance, the observed dataset remains unbiased.

results.title: missing data - Multiple imputation for outcome variables - Cross Validated
results.content: # Multiple imputation for outcome variables. Is there any reason why I can't use the same process to impute missing outcome data? I can probably form a relatively informative imputation model for biomass response ratio given grain response ratio, crop type, and other covariates that I have. Don't forget that you need to make sure to include the outcome in the imputation models for the covariates. If we have access to an auxiliary complete variable that is not part of the model and that is highly correlated with the outcome, imputation can be considerably more efficient than complete case analysis, resulting in more precise estimates and shorter confidence intervals. $\begingroup$ @StefvanBuuren - helpful answer for the most part, but my understanding is that "if we know (or suspect) that the data are MNAR" then imputation cannot solve our problems any more than complete case analysis can. In the first case discussed in @Stef van Buuren's answer, all covariates present but response missing, a complete case analysis implicitly uses the covariate distribution of the complete cases, and imputing the response will make the full observed covariate distribution available. A major issue in missing value imputation is that whether (and how exactly) a model assuming MCAR, MAR, or MNAR is correct is strictly not observable, because it critically depends on the values that are actually missing. What you should be doing is multiple imputation which, for continuous covariates, accounts for the random error you would have observed had you retroactively measured these missing values. Multiple imputation is a process of iteratively generating additive error for conditional mean imputation, so that through 7 or 8 simulated imputations, you can combine models and their errors to get correct estimates of model parameters and their standard errors. If you have jointly missing covariates and outcomes, then there is software in SAS, STATA, and R called multiple imputation via chained equations where "completed" datasets (datasets with imputed values which are treated as fixed and non-random) are generated, model parameters estimated from each complete dataset, and their parameter estimates and standard errors combined using a correct mathematical formation (details in the Van Buuren paper). 2") Including the outcome variable in multiple imputation.
